passage:
Monday. Bhupen, eleven, copied his maths homework from Rajat on the school bus. That evening, when his sister Alka spotted the same wrong answer in both books, he shrugged. "Everyone copies. And Sir gives way too much anyway."
Wednesday. Sir praised Bhupen's neat work in front of the class. Bhupen smiled, but at lunch he couldn't finish his paratha. "It's not cheating if it's just homework," he told Alka that night, though she hadn't said a thing.
Friday. He sat at the table with the new sums and a pencil. "I got question four wrong on my own," he told Alka. "That's okay, right?"

qa.q: Where did Bhupen copy his maths homework?
qa.a: On the school bus.

qa.q: Why did Bhupen say 'It's not cheating' when Alka hadn't said a thing?
qa.a: Bhupen wanted to keep seeing himself as a good kid, so reasons kept coming to quiet the uneasy feeling the copying left.

qa.q: What turning point came on Friday?
qa.a: Bhupen chose to do the sums himself and accept getting question four wrong, trading the excuses for honest work.

qa.q: How might Alka have seen Bhupen's excuses that week?
qa.a: Alka probably noticed the excuses came before she'd said anything, a sign that Bhupen felt uneasy about copying.

grounding: Over a week an eleven-year-old who copied homework piles up excuses that protect his good-kid image, then does the sums himself.

passage:
Sabina, you say everyone copies homework? Let your neighbour Karthik uncle tell you about Class 5, in 1978.
I copied my friend Selvam's English exercise every morning for a month. When my father found out, I had my reasons ready: everyone copies, Miss sets far too many exercises, and anyway English is useless for an engineer. I was very proud of those reasons. I thought they made me a good boy who was simply being clever.
Funny thing: I only thought of them after I'd copied. Never before.
Then came the half-yearly exam. No Selvam in the exam hall. I sat with the paper and could not write one sentence.
So. What were you really going to say about your homework?

qa.q: Whose English exercise did Karthik copy?
qa.a: His friend Selvam's.

qa.q: Why was young Karthik so proud of his reasons?
qa.a: The reasons let him keep seeing himself as a good boy who was just being clever, rather than someone who had copied.

qa.q: What might have helped young Karthik before the half-yearly exam?
qa.a: Doing even a few exercises on his own, and asking the teacher for help when there was too much, would have given him something to write in the exam.

qa.q: How might Sabina hear the question at the end?
qa.a: Sabina may feel gently caught, realising Karthik uncle has guessed that 'everyone copies' was an excuse, not the real story.

grounding: A neighbour recalls how as a boy his reasons for copying homework came only after the act and protected his image as a good boy.

passage:
The band for the wedding next door played until midnight, and Divyansh, ten, had spent the whole evening watching the dancers from the terrace instead of doing his science questions. In the morning, in the rattling school van, he copied Binita's answers on his knee.
When Binita asked, "Why didn't you do them yourself?", Divyansh had his answer ready. "Everyone copies science. Ma'am gives us twenty questions, that's crazy. And nobody could study with that band anyway."
"You could have done them before the band started," Binita said.
Divyansh looked out of the window. "I'm not a cheater. It's just homework," he said, a little too loudly.

qa.q: Where did Divyansh copy Binita's answers?
qa.a: In the rattling school van, on his knee.

qa.q: Why does Divyansh say 'I'm not a cheater' a little too loudly?
qa.a: Divyansh feels guilty and defensive about copying, so he piles up reasons to shield the picture of himself as a good kid.

qa.q: What could Divyansh do the next time an evening looks noisy?
qa.a: Start the science questions before the band begins, or tell Ma'am honestly if it's too much, instead of copying and explaining it away.

qa.q: How might Binita feel about being copied from and then argued with?
qa.a: Binita may feel used and a bit annoyed, since Divyansh took the answers and then blamed everything except himself.

grounding: On a noisy wedding night a ten-year-old skips his homework, copies in the school van, and then produces reasons to stay a good kid in his own eyes.

passage:
During lunch break at his school in Aliganj, Yusuf, ten, slid Abhinav's English worksheet under his own and copied the answers fast, pencil squeaking. His stomach gave a small twist.
That evening his cousin Rehana flipped through his bag and frowned. "These are exactly Abhinav's words."
"So?" Yusuf said, too quickly. "Everyone copies. Half the class copied from Abhinav. And Ma'am gives us four worksheets a day, it's crazy."
Rehana raised an eyebrow. Yusuf kept going. "I'm not a cheater. I'm top three in maths. I just didn't have time, that's all."
The more he explained, the better he felt. By dinner he had nearly convinced himself it was the only sensible thing to do. Still, when he packed his bag for school, he tucked the worksheet deep under his books.

qa.q: Where did Yusuf copy Abhinav's worksheet?
qa.a: During lunch break at his school in Aliganj, sliding it under his own.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf feel better the more he explained?
qa.a: Yusuf felt guilty after copying, and each reason he gave protected his picture of himself as a good student, so the guilt eased the more he explained.

qa.q: What moment could have been a turning point for Yusuf?
qa.a: When Rehana raised an eyebrow, Yusuf could have admitted copying and asked Ma'am for more time; instead he kept adding reasons.

qa.q: How might Rehana see Yusuf's list of reasons?
qa.a: Rehana probably notices that the reasons pile up only after being caught and come out too quickly, so they sound like a defence rather than the real story.

grounding: Shows a child who copied homework producing reasons afterwards, that everyone copies and there is too much work, to keep seeing himself as a good student.

passage:
"Usha, come here a minute."
"What, Appa?"
"Your science answers. Imran's mother showed me his notebook at the gate. Same words. Same spelling mistake in 'photosynthesis'."
"Everybody does it, Appa. Imran copies from me in maths."
"Did you copy?"
"Miss gave us twenty questions! Twenty! Nobody can finish that."
"That's not what I asked."
"And Imran said it was okay. He offered."
"Usha."
"...I copied. But I'm not a bad girl. I do my own work usually."
"I know you're not a bad girl. That's why I'm asking. When did you think of all these reasons?"
Usha, ten, picked at a sofa thread. "Just now, I think."
"Hmm. So what will you do about the twenty questions next time?"

qa.q: What spelling mistake appeared in both notebooks?
qa.a: The same spelling mistake in 'photosynthesis'.

qa.q: Why does Usha keep adding reasons before admitting she copied?
qa.a: Admitting it clashes with seeing herself as a good girl, so reasons like everybody does it, twenty questions and Imran offered protect that picture and ease the shame.

qa.q: What choice by Appa helped Usha get to the truth?
qa.a: Appa didn't argue with each excuse but kept returning to the real question, then asked when the reasons appeared, letting Usha notice they came afterwards.

qa.q: What might Imran's mother have been thinking when she showed the notebook at the gate?
qa.a: She probably wanted the parents to sort it out together rather than blame one child, and may have been worried about what both children were learning.

grounding: Illustrates a child who copied homework defending it with reasons that everyone copies and the work is too much, reasons that arrive after the act to protect her good-kid image.
